title: The Crimson Orchid
subtitle: A locked glasshouse. An empty pot. Twelve missing minutes.
brief: At 8:45, the curator unlocked the public doors and found Marrow House's priceless Crimson Orchid missing. Its ceramic display pot was untouched, and the conservatory alarm never sounded.
Three people were still inside the estate. One of them moved a living plant out of a room that records every opening of its main door.
question: Who took the orchid, and how did it leave the glasshouse?

suspects.name: Nadia Moss
suspects.statement: I misted the east bench until closing. I never touched the potting trolley.

suspects.name: Rohan Pike
suspects.statement: The lights fluttered. I stayed at the fuse cabinet until they steadied.

suspects.name: Celeste Vane
suspects.statement: I waited in the marble lobby. Orchids dislike me almost as much as I dislike humidity.

theories.label: Hidden in a nursery sleeve beneath the potting cart, then passed through the service hatch
Wrapped in a coat and carried through the alarmed main door
Relabelled days earlier and collected as ordinary greenhouse stock

clues.title: One badge, one visit
clues.text: Nadia's badge opened the main door at 8:32 and logged her exit at 8:44. No other door event occurred before the orchid was reported missing.

clues.title: A clean crescent
clues.text: The ceramic display pot contains undisturbed compost and a clean crescent where a removable black nursery sleeve had rested. The orchid was lifted without its display pot.

clues.title: The dry east bench
clues.text: Automatic misting finished at 7:55. The east-bench leaves and floor are bone-dry, contradicting Nadia's account of twelve minutes spent misting there.

clues.title: A damp ring below
clues.text: The potting cart's lower shelf holds a damp crescent, black nursery grit, and one red petal. Its canvas skirt hides the entire shelf from view.

clues.title: The door that is not a door
clues.text: A waist-high service hatch beside the potting cart opens into the loading corridor. It moves supplies but is absent from the alarm's door log.

hints: The alarm log proves how people entered—not necessarily how a plant left.
Compare Nadia's statement with the water log, then follow the black nursery grit.

solution.title: The flower travelled freight class.
solution.explanation: Nadia lifted the orchid in its removable nursery sleeve, hid it behind the potting cart's canvas skirt, and rolled the cart beside the unmonitored service hatch. Her misting story covered the time she needed; the dry bench proves that story false. The damp crescent, nursery grit, and petal trace the orchid to the cart, while the hatch explains how it left without another door event.
proof: The dry bench breaks Nadia's alibi
The cart carries a physical trace of the orchid
The service hatch bypasses the logged door

title: The Letter at Platform Four
subtitle: Sixty seconds of darkness was enough to steal only the words.
brief: A sealed display envelope in the station café held the final page of novelist Vera Bell's unpublished book. During a one-minute blackout, the page vanished. The envelope's red wax seal remained perfect.
The glass case was in view of the counter, the departure board, and a café table. Everyone insists the blackout caught them where they stood.
question: Who stole the page, and how was the intact seal defeated?

suspects.name: Milo Penn
suspects.statement: I stayed behind the till. In the dark, I could barely find the candles.

suspects.name: June Sato
suspects.statement: I was scanning my platform ticket when the lights failed.

suspects.name: Arun Bell
suspects.statement: I watched the departure clock. I wanted the page, but not badly enough to miss my train.

theories.label: Opened the case's rear service panel and removed the page without touching the envelope seal
Made a duplicate wax seal, opened the envelope, and resealed it during the blackout
Pulled the page through a narrow gap in the front glass with wire

clues.title: A truly intact seal
clues.text: The wax bears Vera Bell's tiny fingerprint and has no reheating marks. The envelope was not opened after it entered the case.

clues.title: Built for quick changes
clues.text: The display has a rear service panel for replacing menus. It opens with the same square pantry key kept on the café manager's ring.

clues.title: A theatrical blackout
clues.text: Nothing failed. The café's lighting breaker was manually lowered. It sits eighteen centimetres below the till.

clues.title: Coffee behind the case
clues.text: A fresh dark-coffee ring marks the hidden rear shelf. Milo drinks black coffee; June ordered tea and Arun carried no cup.

clues.title: Two clocks agree
clues.text: June's platform scanner registered at 6:14:22. Arun's train gate opened under camera at 6:14:31. Both were outside the café before the lights returned.

hints: An intact envelope does not mean an intact display case.
Only one person could reach both the breaker and the square pantry key without moving from his claimed position.

solution.title: The seal was never the lock.
solution.explanation: Milo staged the blackout from the breaker beneath his till, used his square pantry key on the case's rear panel, and slid the manuscript page out of the still-sealed envelope through its open top. The fresh coffee ring places him behind the case. June and Arun were both captured outside the café during the crucial minute.
proof: The seal was never disturbed
Milo controlled the breaker and service key
His coffee marks the concealed access point

title: The Silent Bell
subtitle: The museum alarm trusted weight. The thief trusted theatre paint.
brief: The Aster Museum's silver Pilgrim Bell disappeared from a pressure-alarmed plinth. The alarm never changed weight, and the object under the glass looked correct until a curator noticed it made no sound.
The silent object is a painted brass rehearsal bell. Someone prepared a replacement and balanced it precisely.
question: Who made the substitution, and how was the weight alarm fooled?

suspects.name: Inez Vale
suspects.statement: I polished the real bell on Tuesday. I have not handled the rehearsal pieces this month.

suspects.name: Bo Mercer
suspects.statement: My round passed the east gallery every ten minutes. The display never looked disturbed.

suspects.name: Mae Aster
suspects.statement: I donated it. Selling it would be a rather circular form of generosity.

theories.label: Swapped in a painted rehearsal bell weighted internally with conservation lead
Braced the pressure plate from beneath while removing the bell
Held the weight sensor in place with a strong magnet during the theft

clues.title: Exact to the gram
clues.text: The false bell weighs 1,842 grams—the exact registered weight of the original. A loose object shifts inside its hollow base.

clues.title: A hidden half-moon
clues.text: Imaging reveals a crescent of soft lead screwed inside the replica. The lead has been cut with fine conservation shears.

clues.title: Rehearsal piece 3B
clues.text: Inez signed out rehearsal bell 3B on Wednesday for 'surface comparison.' She returned it Thursday morning.

clues.title: Silver over brass
clues.text: A metallic paint flake under Inez's drying rack matches the replica's fresh coating. It contains the museum workshop's rare mica binder.

clues.title: A narrow workshop window
clues.text: Bo's mechanical checkpoint card confirms every round. Mae was speaking on the gallery stage when Inez alone wheeled a covered conservation crate past the plinth.

hints: The alarm did exactly what it was designed to do: notice a change in weight.
Ask who had access to the replica, the lead, the right shears, and the matching paint.

solution.title: A perfect weight, and a hollow alibi.
solution.explanation: Inez prepared rehearsal bell 3B with silver paint and a carefully cut crescent of conservation lead until it matched the Pilgrim Bell gram for gram. During her authorised crate movement, she exchanged the objects. The pressure alarm saw no change. The loan signature, workshop-only mica paint, and shear-cut lead make the preparation uniquely hers.
proof: The replica was tuned to the alarm's exact weight
Workshop materials link the preparation to Inez
Her crate supplied the opportunity

title: The Midnight Broadcast
subtitle: The ending leaked before the actors spoke it aloud.
brief: At 11:48, minutes before WNR's live mystery drama, a rival station broadcast the secret final line. Only three numbered script copies existed, and all three were still in their owners' hands.
The rival received a typed note, not a photograph. Someone copied the ending without surrendering their script.
question: Who leaked the ending, and what copying trick did they use?

suspects.name: Ada North
suspects.statement: My script stayed on my music stand while I warmed up in Studio B.

suspects.name: Sol Reed
suspects.statement: I was cueing shellac effects. I heard the final line for the first time on air.

suspects.name: Viola Crane
suspects.statement: My courtesy copy remained sealed in its blue folder. I never even read the thing.

theories.label: Typed the ending with carbon paper hidden beneath the sheet, creating a second copy in one pass
Recorded rehearsal through the studio vent and transcribed the final line
Reconstructed the ending from sound-effect cues and actor entrances

clues.title: A private correction
clues.text: The leaked line includes 'the harbour keeps its dead'—a correction handwritten only on copy C, Viola's sponsor copy. Copies A and B still say 'secrets.'

clues.title: Sealed, but not untouched
clues.text: Viola's folder seal is intact. Its bottom edge, however, was never glued; the script slides out cleanly without breaking the seal.

clues.title: The ghost beneath the words
clues.text: The rival's note carries faint blue pressure marks behind the black letters. They are characteristic of a carbon sheet placed under the typed page.

clues.title: A chipped capital V
clues.text: The note's capital V has a missing left serif. The same defect appears on the sponsor lounge typewriter and nowhere else in WNR.

clues.title: One brief outside line
clues.text: At 11:42, the sponsor lounge placed a forty-second call to the rival station's news desk. Viola signed the room register at 11:39.

hints: The unique corrected wording identifies which script supplied the leak.
The note was produced by a particular machine, and its pale blue marks reveal a second sheet.

solution.title: Copy C made copy D.
solution.explanation: Viola slid copy C through the unglued bottom of its ceremonial folder, typed the corrected final line in the sponsor lounge with carbon paper beneath it, and phoned the duplicate to WNR's rival. The unique correction identifies her script; the chipped V identifies her typewriter; the blue pressure marks reveal the carbon copy.
proof: Only Viola's copy contains the leaked correction
The sponsor typewriter left its broken-serif signature
The lounge call delivered the line

title: Cabin Nine
subtitle: A jewel vanished from a room no stranger entered.
brief: Journalist Noor Dey reported her emerald brooch stolen from locked Cabin Nine while she dined two cars away. The corridor seal was unbroken, the window opens only eight centimetres, and the porter retained his passkey.
At 1:40, a green stone was found beneath Noor's washbasin. She called it proof that a thief had fumbled the jewel while escaping.
question: Who engineered the impossible theft, and what was the real aim?

suspects.name: Noor Dey
suspects.statement: The brooch was on my washstand. Someone entered despite the seal—I cannot explain it.

suspects.name: Elias Ward
suspects.statement: My passkey stayed chained to my belt. I sealed the corridor myself.

suspects.name: Sable Fox
suspects.statement: An impossible room is usually a very possible lie. This one is not my trick.

theories.label: Replaced the real brooch with paste, disposed of the fake stone, and staged an insurance claim
Hooked the brooch through the narrow window from the carriage platform
Made a wax impression of the porter's passkey and entered before the corridor was sealed

clues.title: Glass under the basin
clues.text: The loose green stone scratches at hardness 5.5. Emerald should score 7.5 or higher. The recovered stone is bottle glass.

clues.title: A deliberate fracture
clues.text: The clasp found on the washstand has parallel file marks and fresh brass beneath them. It was weakened before the train departed.

clues.title: Insured in a hurry
clues.text: Noor tripled the brooch's insurance yesterday afternoon and requested coverage beginning precisely at midnight.

clues.title: An emerald heading south
clues.text: A dealer in the previous city logged the real brooch's maker mark at 4:10 PM—two hours before Noor boarded the Night Meridian.

clues.title: The locked room holds
clues.text: The numbered paper seal, window soot, and key chain are all intact. There is no physical evidence that anyone entered Cabin Nine after dinner.

hints: Start by asking whether the recovered stone was ever part of an emerald brooch.
The real jewel's timeline ends before the train journey begins.

solution.title: There was no theft aboard the train.
solution.explanation: Noor sold or pledged the real brooch before boarding, weakened a cheap replica's clasp, and dropped its glass stone beneath the basin. She then reported an impossible locked-cabin theft to activate newly increased insurance. The dealer's maker-mark record places the real jewel off the train, and every cabin seal confirms that no intruder was needed.
proof: The recovered 'emerald' is bottle glass
The clasp was prepared to fail
The real brooch was logged in another city

title: The Saffron Impression
subtitle: The recipe never left its drawer. Its shadow did.
brief: Sunroom Bakery locked its prize saffron-bun recipe in a desk at closing. At dawn, a rival shop displayed the exact recipe—including its strange pinch of black salt. The drawer's paper seal was intact.
Three afternoon visitors stood beside the recipe before it was locked away. One copied it without a camera, a key, or even a pencil.
question: Who copied the recipe, and what ordinary material carried the words away?

suspects.name: Pippa Lo
suspects.statement: I weighed saffron at the far counter. I know most of the recipe already, but not the salt.

suspects.name: Basil Crow
suspects.statement: I wrote tasting notes beside the desk. Trade secrets make terribly dry reading.

suspects.name: Emi Rose
suspects.statement: I set down a damp bouquet, collected my invoice, and left. I never opened a drawer.

theories.label: Pressed damp waxed bouquet paper onto the violet-pencil recipe and read the reversed transfer later
Made a pencil rubbing of indentations left on the desk blotter
Deduced every quantity by tasting a finished bun and guessing the method

clues.title: A secret that stayed put
clues.text: The recipe card remains inside the desk. Its numbered paper seal and old lock dust are undisturbed. The information—not the card—was stolen.

clues.title: Violet pencil
clues.text: The baker writes with a soft violet copying pencil. When dampened, its pigment transfers readily onto paper pressed against it.

clues.title: Fern-shaped moisture
clues.text: The recipe card bears a faint damp outline shaped like fern leaves. Emi's bouquet used the same fern as packing greenery.

clues.title: Letters in reverse
clues.text: Beneath the rival baker's black-ink copy are faint reversed violet words: 'black salt, one pinch.' They read correctly in a mirror.

clues.title: One sheet too few
clues.text: Emi's delivery roll is waxed on one side and missing its final numbered sheet. A torn corner in her invoice book carries violet pigment.

hints: The reversed words were transferred by contact, not written from memory.
Violet copying pencil, moisture, and one missing sheet of bouquet paper form a complete copying method.

solution.title: The bouquet took an impression.
solution.explanation: Emi laid damp waxed wrapping over the face-up recipe while collecting her invoice. Moisture activated the soft violet copying pencil, leaving a reversed impression on the paper. She removed that sheet with the bouquet and read it in a mirror. The fern-shaped moisture mark, reversed violet text, and missing numbered paper all trace the copy to her.
proof: The recipe itself never left the sealed drawer
The rival's note preserves a reversed violet transfer
Emi's damp wrapping supplied the copying surface

title: The Clockmaker's Tuesday
subtitle: At quarter past four, a clock that cannot chime gave someone away.
brief: A prototype silver pocket watch vanished from a velvet tray behind the shop counter. The front door stayed in view, no one crossed the counter gate, and the tray glass was found closed.
Three visitors stood close enough to admire the watch. Only one describes a sound the shop could never make.
question: Who took the watch, and how did they lift it without crossing the counter?

suspects.name: Elian Morrow
suspects.statement: I stepped out for tea at ten past four and returned before the hour.

suspects.name: Ruth Kline
suspects.statement: I signed the delivery book, set two boxes down, and left at 4:14.

suspects.name: August Vale
suspects.statement: I remained by the front case. I distinctly heard the shop clock chime quarter past four.

theories.label: Used a magnet concealed in a hollow cane to lift the watch by its steel chain
Lowered an open parcel over the tray and trapped the watch inside it
Looped thread through the counter grille and dragged the watch across the velvet

clues.title: No quarter chime
clues.text: The regulator clock strikes only on the hour. Its movement has no quarter-chime train and never has. August's vivid 4:15 memory is invented.

clues.title: A round absence
clues.text: Dust on the glass above the tray shows a clean circular mark, 28 millimetres wide—the exact diameter of August's silver cane ferrule.

clues.title: The lid lifts upward
clues.text: The tray's glass lid is not locked. From the customer side, a long object can raise it through the ornamental brass grille.

clues.title: North follows the cane
clues.text: A watchmaker's compass swings forty degrees when August's cane passes. The ferrule conceals a strong horseshoe magnet.

clues.title: One link left behind
clues.text: A broken steel chain link clings inside the magnetised ferrule. The prototype's silver case is non-magnetic, but its safety chain is steel.

hints: August supplies a precise time marker, but verify whether the clock could supply it.
The watch case is silver; another attached part would still answer a magnet.

solution.title: The cane had an attraction to fine watches.
solution.explanation: August invented the quarter chime to anchor his false alibi. From the customer side, he fed his hollow cane through the brass grille, lifted the unlocked glass lid, and caught the watch's steel safety chain with the concealed magnet. The circular dust mark fixes the cane above the tray, and the broken chain link remains attached to the ferrule.
proof: August describes a chime the clock cannot make
His cane matches the circular trace on the glass
Its hidden magnet holds the watch's broken chain link
